## Introduction

Cutaneous beta- and gamma-HPVs act more like normal skin flora than disease-causing pathogens. They are acquired early in life, are ubiquitous in healthy adults, and persist as asymptomatic, low-level infections [@antonsson2000; @doorbar2023] that expand when host immunity fails [@hou2026]. At the DNA level the reservoir is large and well mapped: shotgun metagenomics detected HPV in 61.3% of healthy skin samples [@ma2014], skin swabs found beta-HPV in 92% of adults [@rollison2019sites], and the community spans 396 types, 229 of them previously unknown [@bzhalava2014]. DNA detection alone, however, cannot show whether any of these genomes are transcribed.

This matters because beta-HPV is a suspected cofactor in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), particularly among organ transplant recipients [@howley2015; @rollison2019]. Three distinct, mutually compatible models account for this role from the same evidence. Under hit-and-run, beta-HPV acts synergistically with ultraviolet radiation, immunosuppression, or chronic inflammation during early tumorigenesis but becomes dispensable once the tumor is established [@viarisio2018; @dorfer2021]. This model proposes only that the virus is no longer required, not that it is actively cleared, so viral activity declines only where a mechanism for viral loss exists. The protective-immunity model instead proposes that T-cell responses against commensal papillomaviruses actively suppress skin carcinogenesis, so viral loss reflects immune-mediated selection rather than dispensability [@strickley2019; @lambert2021; @strickley2021; @son2025]. A third model requires neither premise: transcriptional silence is the viral default, because the beta-HPV genome uses E8\^E2 to repress its own expression and transformation requires inactivating that repressor [@rehm2022]. All three therefore predict declining viral activity from healthy skin to carcinoma, so measuring that decline more precisely cannot distinguish among them.

Studies directly testing whether HPV is transcribed in cSCC have mostly found little or no viral transcription. The original cSCC transcriptome study detected no viral transcripts [@arron2011], nor did an analysis of 12 skin lesions at a median depth of 66 million reads [@hultin2019]. A study of 345 posttransplant tumors at 35 million reads identified transcription in only 15 cases [@arroyomuhr2021], and 23 risk-stratified biopsies showed none despite a 64% DNA positivity rate [@vandiver2021]. E6/E7 mRNA in situ hybridization showed expression in just 0.9% of 225 nonanogenital cSCCs [@fujimoto2019]. The literature is not unanimous: in situ hybridization detected epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV)-associated HPV transcripts in 4 of 11 PCR-positive transplant cSCCs [@purdie2005]. Across these studies, sample sizes were modest, from 11 to 345 specimens; four of the five had no comparison group of unselected skin, so they cannot establish how often HPV is transcribed in carcinoma relative to healthy skin; the largest cohort was restricted to formalin-fixed transplant tissue; and none assessed productive viral replication.

Public sequencing archives make such a large-scale comparison possible. Standard RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) pipelines align reads to the human reference genome and discard those that do not map. Viral reads go with them, but remain in the raw data deposited in public repositories and can be recovered by targeted reanalysis [@edgar2022]. The strategy has already been applied to skin datasets [@leiendecker2023; @bhargava2025], but carries technical pitfalls: HeLa-derived HPV18 extensively contaminates archived sequencing data [@cantalupo2015; @kazemian2015; @adey2013], and sequencing depth and library chemistry constrain detection sensitivity. Here we reanalyzed public human RNA-seq data spanning healthy skin, warts, and skin cancer to determine how often cutaneous HPV is transcribed, which types are present, and whether these infections are productive.
